content: Healthcare providers who deliver care to children and adolescents play a critical role in recognizing and managing tuberculosis (TB). The concept of task-shifting, as highlighted by the Guideline Development Group (GDG), is an essential factor in implementing TB care strategies. Family-centered and integrated care is a key approach in child health, although its definition remains somewhat unclear. This model is closely related to the broader concept of patient-centered care. According to the End TB Strategy, patient-centered care systematically evaluates and addresses the needs and expectations of patients. Depending on the patient’s needs, educational, emotional, and economic support should be provided to help them complete the diagnostic process and the full course of prescribed treatment. Family-centered care also involves household-level interventions, such as identifying family members who may need TB evaluation, preventive therapy (TPT), or treatment support. Since the concept of family-centered, integrated care may vary by setting, it is crucial to first define how it applies to the specific context where care will be implemented. Implementation strategies should be tailored to the country or region, taking into account social, cultural, and societal values. The national TB program, in collaboration with other relevant programs, should define and develop a package of TB services. This package should address capacity needs for national programs interested in adopting proposed interventions and should ideally be based on family and community perceptions of the ideal family-centered care model. Integration can begin within families by equipping them with the knowledge to recognize TB symptoms, understand the importance of contact history, seek timely healthcare, and reduce TB-related stigma. High-yield entry points within the health system, such as malnutrition clinics, antenatal care (ANC), immunization programs, inpatient sites, and HIV or general pediatric clinics, provide opportunities to integrate child and adolescent TB services. Ideally, TB care should be fully integrated into general health services rather than relying solely on coordination between separate programs. However, defining optimal patient flow between services and strengthening links between child health entry points and TB clinics remain essential, particularly in facilities where services are physically separated. Pilot programs may be considered during the early phases of implementation, with subsequent evaluation and scaling up as needed. Factors such as baseline health infrastructure, regulatory frameworks, financing, human resource requirements, and community needs should be carefully assessed. Differentiated service delivery (DSD), a person-centered approach initially developed for HIV care, can also be applied to TB services. This approach simplifies and adapts care to meet the needs of individuals while optimizing health system resources. Examples of DSD for children and adolescents at risk of or diagnosed with TB are provided in the World Health Organization’s operational handbook. Monitoring and evaluation are critical for the successful implementation of decentralized, family-centered, and integrated TB services. National TB programs must identify and address capacity needs for proposed interventions. Enhanced data collection on child and adolescent TB, including bacteriological confirmation rates, clinical diagnoses, and TPT initiation and completion rates, is essential. Data should be disaggregated by sex to evaluate the impact on gender equity. Evaluating service quality, patient satisfaction, and outcomes such as treatment success and mental health is also important. Research priorities include assessing the effectiveness of interventions to improve treatment adherence, patient support, and supervision, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. Cost-effectiveness analyses of incentives, decentralized care, and family-centered models are needed. Additionally, research should explore the acceptability and feasibility of these approaches from the perspectives of patients, caregivers, and providers. Addressing stigma, mental health outcomes, and community perceptions of TB care and prevention for children and adolescents is also vital.
